The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the [[Imperial House of Japan|imperial dynasty]], making both clans distant relatives. The Minamoto were one of [[Japanese clans|four great noble clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the [[Heian period]]—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the [[Tachibana clan (kuge)|Tachibana]]. Thus, descendants of the Minamoto today still hold important positions in the [[Politics of Japan|politics]], [[Economy of Japan|economy]], [[Education in Japan|education]], and [[Culture of Japan|culture]] of [[Modern Japan|modern]] [[Japan|Japanese society]]. == History == [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|right|[[Seiryō-ji]], a temple in [[Kyoto]], was once a villa of [[Minamoto no Tōru|Minamoto no Toru]] (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji]] [[File:Map-of-Japan-1183-Heian-Genpei-War.png|thumb|The domain of the Minamoto clan in Japan (1183) during the [[Genpei War]] ]] The first emperor to grant the surname Minamoto was [[Minamoto no Makoto]], seventh son of Emperor Saga.Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press. The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the [[Seiwa Genji]], descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]] (897–961), a grandson of Emperor Seiwa. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka]] (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern [[Kyoto|Kyōto]]).{{rp|240–241}} Mitsunaka's eldest son, [[Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] (948–1021), became the protégé of [[Fujiwara no Michinaga]]; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of [[Taira no Tadatsune]] in 1032. Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including [[Minamoto no Tameyoshi]]. During the [[Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, [[Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]] and [[Emperor Toba|Toba]] and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the [[Genpei War]], Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192 he received the title ''[[shōgun]]'' and set up the first ''[[bakufu]]'' at [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]].{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} The later [[Ashikaga clan|Ashikaga]] (founders of the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]), [[Nitta family|Nitta]], and [[Takeda family|Takeda]] clans claim descent from the Seiwa Genji.{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA53|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|pages=53|language=en}}{{Cite book|last=Zöllner|first=Reinhard|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SwUvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=Die Ludowinger und die Takeda: Feudale Herrschaft in Thüringen und Kai no kuni|date=2018-02-15|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-7448-8682-6|pages=127|language=de}} The [[protagonist]] of the classical Japanese novel ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', [[Hikaru Genji]], was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The [[Genpei War]] is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last=Watson|first=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == [[File:Genealogy-of-the-Minamoto-Clan-Utagawa-Kuniyoshi.png|thumb|300px|Genealogy of the Minamoto clan, [[ukiyo-e]] by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]]] Even within royalty there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}} ("[having the] ability to advance", ''i.e.'', eligible to become the new Emperor), who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}} ("great" or "major"), who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the royal class (and therefore outranked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known [[Bhikkhu|monks]] of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favor of a [[dharma name]]). There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after the emperor from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few produced and no descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of [[Emperor Saga]]. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''[[Japanese name|uji]]'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, Makoto, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]] took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early [[Heian period]]. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. Clans such as the [[Watanabe]], [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji. Noted Saga Genji and descendants include: * [[Minamoto no Makoto|Makoto]], seventh son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiromu|Hiromu]], eighth son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Hitoshi|Hitoshi]], grandson of Hiromu * [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Okoru|Okoru]], first son of Tokiwa * [[Minamoto no Sadamu|Sadamu]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Shitagō|Shitagō]], great-grandson of Sadamu * [[Minamoto no Hiroshi|Hiroshi]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]], son of the Emperor ** [[Anbō]] (secular name Minamoto no Shitagō), great-grandson of Tōru ** [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] (his official name was Minamoto no Tsuna, who resided at Watanabe in Settsu province, and took the name of the place), great-great-grandson of Tōru *** [[Matsuura Hisashi]], great-grandson of Tsuna ** [[Minamoto no Koreshige|Koreshige]], grandson of Tōru *** [[Minamoto no Mitsusue|Mitsusue]], great-great-grandson of Koreshige * [[Minamoto no Tsutomu|Tsutomu]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku|Hiraku]], son of the Emperor History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime|Kiyohime]], Sadahime, and Yoshihime), but few records concerning his daughters are known. ===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of [[Emperor Ninmyō]]. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru|Masaru]] and [[Minamoto no Hikaru|Hikaru]] were [[udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was Minamoto no Atsushi, adoptive father of the Saga Genji's [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] and father of the Seiwa Genji's [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Mitsunaka]]'s wife. ===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Montoku]]. Among them, [[Minamoto no Yoshiari|Yoshiari]] was a [[sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]]. ===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. The most numerous of them were those descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]], son of [[Prince Sadazumi]]. [[Minamoto no Yoshiie|Hachimantarō Yoshiie]] of the [[Kawachi Genji]] was a leader of a ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. His descendants set up the [[Kamakura shogunate]], making his a prestigious pedigree claimed by many ''buke'', particularly for the direct descendants in the [[Ashikaga clan]] (that set up the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]) and the rival [[Nitta clan]]. Centuries later, [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Yōzei]]. While [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]] is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by [[Hoshino Hisashi]]) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Yōzei rather than of Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behavior, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kōkō]]. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''[[busshi]]'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Uda]]. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], [[Minamoto no Masanobu|Masanobu]] and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu|Shigenobu]] became ''[[sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]'' the [[Sasaki clan]] of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Daigo]]. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]]. ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]''). ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa]] son [[Prince Mochihito|Mochihito-ō]] (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the [[Genpei War]], he was declassed (renamed "Minamoto no Mochimitsu") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]]. ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. Hisaaki's sons [[Prince Morikuni]] (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually [[Nijō Michihira]]'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''[[dainagon]]''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == See also == *[[History of Japan]] *[[Taira clan]] ==References== ==External links== {{commons category|Minamoto clan}} *[http://samurai-archives.com/HeianPeriod.html Heian Period: Minamoto Clan history] [[Category:Minamoto clan| ]] [[Category:Heian period]]

{{Short description|Prominent noble family in feudal Japan}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname = Minamoto |surname nihongo = {{Nobold|源}} |image = Sasa Rindo.svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (emblem)|''mon'']]) of the Minamoto clan |home province = Various |parent house = [[File:Imperial Seal of Japan.svg|15px]] [[Imperial House of Japan]] |titles = Various |founder = Various; [[Minamoto no Makoto]] (first recorded) |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = {{Plainlist| * [[Saga Genji]] * [[Ninmyō Genji]] * [[Montoku Genji]] * [[Seiwa Genji]] * [[Yōzei Genji]] * [[Kōkō Genji]] * [[Uda Genji]] * [[Daigo Genji]] * Murakami Genji * [[Reizei Genji]] * [[Kazan Genji]] * [[Sanjō Genji]] * [[Go-Sanjō Genji]] * [[Go-Shirakawa Genji]] * [[Juntoku Genji]] * [[Go-Saga Genji]] * [[Go-Fusakusa Genji]] * [[Ōgimachi Genji]]}} }}
{{nihongo|'''Minamoto'''|源}} was one of the surnames bestowed by the [[Emperors of Japan]] upon members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|imperial family]] who were excluded from the line of succession and demoted into the ranks of the nobility from 1192 to 1333.<ref>"...the Minamoto (1192-1333)" Warrior Rule in Japan, page 11. Cambridge University Press.</ref> The practice was most prevalent during the [[Heian period]] (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the [[Sengoku period]]. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the imperial dynasty, making both clans distant relatives. The Minamoto clan is also called the {{nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏}}, or less frequently, the {{nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家}}, using the [[on'yomi]] reading for Minamoto.
The Minamoto were one of four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the Heian period—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the [[Tachibana clan (kuge)|Tachibana]].
== History == [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|right|[[Seiryō-ji]], a temple in [[Kyoto]], was once a villa of [[Minamoto no Tōru|Minamoto no Toru]] (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji]] [[File:Map-of-Japan-1183-Heian-Genpei-War.png|thumb|The domain of the Minamoto clan in Japan (1183) during the [[Genpei War]] ]]
The first emperor to grant the surname Minamoto was [[Minamoto no Makoto]], seventh son of Emperor Saga.<ref>Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press.</ref>
The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the [[Seiwa Genji]], descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]] (897–961), a grandson of Emperor Seiwa. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka]] (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern [[Kyoto|Kyōto]]).<ref name="Sansom" />{{rp|240–241}}
Mitsunaka's eldest son, [[Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] (948–1021), became the protégé of [[Fujiwara no Michinaga]]; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of [[Taira no Tadatsune]] in 1032. Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.<ref name=Sansom>{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}}</ref>
The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including [[Minamoto no Tameyoshi]]. During the [[Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, [[Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], died in battle.<ref name=Sansom/>{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]] and [[Emperor Toba|Toba]] and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the [[Genpei War]], Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192 he received the title ''[[shōgun]]'' and set up the first ''[[bakufu]]'' at [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]].<ref name=Sansom/>{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}}
The later [[Ashikaga clan|Ashikaga]] (founders of the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]), [[Nitta family|Nitta]], and [[Takeda family|Takeda]] clans claim descent from the Seiwa Genji.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA53|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|pages=53|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Zöllner|first=Reinhard|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SwUvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=Die Ludowinger und die Takeda: Feudale Herrschaft in Thüringen und Kai no kuni|date=2018-02-15|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-7448-8682-6|pages=127|language=de}}</ref>
The [[protagonist]] of the classical Japanese novel ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', [[Hikaru Genji]], was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer.
The [[Genpei War]] is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'' (''Heike Monogatari'').<ref>{{Cite book|last=Watson|first=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}}</ref>
== Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == [[File:Genealogy-of-the-Minamoto-Clan-Utagawa-Kuniyoshi.png|thumb|300px|Genealogy of the Minamoto clan, [[ukiyo-e]] by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]]]
Even within royalty there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}} ("[having the] ability to advance", ''i.e.'', eligible to become the new Emperor), who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}} ("great" or "major"), who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the royal class (and therefore outranked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession.
Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known [[Bhikkhu|monks]] of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favor of a [[dharma name]]).
There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after the emperor from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few produced and no descendants.
===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of [[Emperor Saga]]. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''[[Japanese name|uji]]'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, Makoto, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]] took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early [[Heian period]]. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. Clans such as the [[Watanabe]], [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji.
Noted Saga Genji and descendants include: * [[Minamoto no Makoto|Makoto]], seventh son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiromu|Hiromu]], eighth son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Hitoshi|Hitoshi]], grandson of Hiromu * [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Okoru|Okoru]], first son of Tokiwa * [[Minamoto no Sadamu|Sadamu]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Shitagō|Shitagō]], great-grandson of Sadamu * [[Minamoto no Hiroshi|Hiroshi]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]], son of the Emperor ** [[Anbō]] (secular name Minamoto no Shitagō), great-grandson of Tōru ** [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] (his official name was Minamoto no Tsuna, who resided at Watanabe in Settsu province, and took the name of the place), great-great-grandson of Tōru *** [[Matsuura Hisashi]], great-grandson of Tsuna ** [[Minamoto no Koreshige|Koreshige]], grandson of Tōru *** [[Minamoto no Mitsusue|Mitsusue]], great-great-grandson of Koreshige * [[Minamoto no Tsutomu|Tsutomu]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku|Hiraku]], son of the Emperor
History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime|Kiyohime]], Sadahime, and Yoshihime), but few records concerning his daughters are known.
===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of [[Emperor Ninmyō]]. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru|Masaru]] and [[Minamoto no Hikaru|Hikaru]] were [[udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was Minamoto no Atsushi, adoptive father of the Saga Genji's [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] and father of the Seiwa Genji's [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Mitsunaka]]'s wife.
===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Montoku]]. Among them, [[Minamoto no Yoshiari|Yoshiari]] was a [[sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]].
===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. Centuries later, [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan.
===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Yōzei]]. ===Kōkō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kōkō]]. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop.
===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Uda]]. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], [[Minamoto no Masanobu|Masanobu]] and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu|Shigenobu]] became ''[[sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]'' the [[Sasaki clan]] of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]].
===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Daigo]]. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician.
===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny.
===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive.
===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]].
===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily.
===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]'').

===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]].
===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Fukakusa]]'s son [[Prince Hisaaki]] (the eighth ''[[shōgun]]'' of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]].

Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including [[Minamoto no Tameyoshi]]. During the [[Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, [[Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]] and [[Emperor Toba|Toba]] and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the [[Genpei War]], Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192 he received the title ''[[shōgun]]'' and set up the first ''[[bakufu]]'' at [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]].{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} The later [[Ashikaga clan|Ashikaga]] (founders of the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]), [[Nitta family|Nitta]], and [[Takeda family|Takeda]] clans claim descent from the Seiwa Genji.{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA53|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|pages=53|language=en}}{{Cite book|last=Zöllner|first=Reinhard|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SwUvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=Die Ludowinger und die Takeda: Feudale Herrschaft in Thüringen und Kai no kuni|date=2018-02-15|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-7448-8682-6|pages=127|language=de}} The [[protagonist]] of the classical Japanese novel ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', [[Hikaru Genji]], was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The [[Genpei War]] is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last=Watson|first=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} [[File:Murasaki-Shikibu-composing-Genji-Monogatari.png|left|thumb|236x236px|[[Murasaki Shikibu]] composing ''Genji Monogatari'' ([[The Tale of Genji]])]] == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == [[File:Genealogy-of-the-Minamoto-Clan-Utagawa-Kuniyoshi.png|thumb|300px|Genealogy of the Minamoto clan, [[ukiyo-e]] by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]]] Even within royalty there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}} ("[having the] ability to advance", ''i.e.'', eligible to become the new Emperor), who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}} ("great" or "major"), who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the royal class (and therefore outranked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known [[Bhikkhu|monks]] of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favor of a [[dharma name]]). There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after the emperor from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few produced and no descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of [[Emperor Saga]]. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''[[Japanese name|uji]]'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, Makoto, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]] took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early [[Heian period]]. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. Clans such as the [[Watanabe]], [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji. Noted Saga Genji and descendants include: * [[Minamoto no Makoto|Makoto]], seventh son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiromu|Hiromu]], eighth son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Hitoshi|Hitoshi]], grandson of Hiromu * [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Okoru|Okoru]], first son of Tokiwa * [[Minamoto no Sadamu|Sadamu]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Shitagō|Shitagō]], great-grandson of Sadamu * [[Minamoto no Hiroshi|Hiroshi]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]], son of the Emperor ** [[Anbō]] (secular name Minamoto no Shitagō), great-grandson of Tōru ** [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] (his official name was Minamoto no Tsuna, who resided at Watanabe in Settsu province, and took the name of the place), great-great-grandson of Tōru *** [[Matsuura Hisashi]], great-grandson of Tsuna ** [[Minamoto no Koreshige|Koreshige]], grandson of Tōru *** [[Minamoto no Mitsusue|Mitsusue]], great-great-grandson of Koreshige * [[Minamoto no Tsutomu|Tsutomu]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku|Hiraku]], son of the Emperor History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime|Kiyohime]], Sadahime, and Yoshihime), but few records concerning his daughters are known. ===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of [[Emperor Ninmyō]]. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru|Masaru]] and [[Minamoto no Hikaru|Hikaru]] were [[udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was Minamoto no Atsushi, adoptive father of the Saga Genji's [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] and father of the Seiwa Genji's [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Mitsunaka]]'s wife. ===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Montoku]]. Among them, [[Minamoto no Yoshiari|Yoshiari]] was a [[sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]]. ===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. The most numerous of them were those descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]], son of [[Prince Sadazumi]]. [[Minamoto no Yoshiie|Hachimantarō Yoshiie]] of the [[Kawachi Genji]] was a leader of a ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. His descendants set up the [[Kamakura shogunate]], making his a prestigious pedigree claimed by many ''buke'', particularly for the direct descendants in the [[Ashikaga clan]] (that set up the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]) and the rival [[Nitta clan]]. Centuries later, [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Yōzei]]. While [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]] is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by [[Hoshino Hisashi]]) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Yōzei rather than of Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behavior, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kōkō]]. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''[[busshi]]'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Uda]]. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], [[Minamoto no Masanobu|Masanobu]] and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu|Shigenobu]] became ''[[sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]'' the [[Sasaki clan]] of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Daigo]]. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]]. ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]''). ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa]] son [[Prince Mochihito|Mochihito-ō]] (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the [[Genpei War]], he was declassed (renamed "Minamoto no Mochimitsu") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]]. ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''[[shōgun]]'' (the seventh of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]) at a young age, and was renamed "Minamoto no Koreyasu" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Fukakusa]]'s son [[Prince Hisaaki]] (the eighth ''[[shōgun]]'' of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]). Hisaaki's sons [[Prince Morikuni]] (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually [[Nijō Michihira]]'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''[[dainagon]]''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == See also == *[[History of Japan]] *[[Japanese clans]] *[[Japanese name]] *[[Minamoto (surname)]] *[[Taira clan]] *[[Genpei War|Genpei war]] *[[Fujiwara clan]] ==References== ==External links== {{commons category|Minamoto clan}} *[http://samurai-archives.com/HeianPeriod.html Heian Period: Minamoto Clan history] [[Category:Minamoto clan| ]] [[Category:Heian period]] [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]]

Cambridge University Press. The practice was most prevalent during the [[Heian period]] (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the [[Sengoku period]]. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the imperial dynasty, making both clans distant relatives. The Minamoto clan is also called the {{nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏}}, or less frequently, the {{nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家}}, using the [[on'yomi]] reading for Minamoto. The Minamoto were one of four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the [[Heian period]]—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the [[Tachibana clan (kuge)|Tachibana]]. == History == [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|right|[[Seiryō-ji]], a temple in [[Kyoto]], was once a villa of [[Minamoto no Tōru|Minamoto no Toru]] (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji]] [[File:Map-of-Japan-1183-Heian-Genpei-War.png|thumb|The domain of the Minamoto clan in Japan (1183) during the [[Genpei War]] ]] The first emperor to grant the surname Minamoto was [[Minamoto no Makoto]], seventh son of [[Emperor Saga]].Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]]. ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]''). ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa]] son [[Prince Mochihito|Mochihito-ō]] (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the [[Genpei War]], he was declassed (renamed "Minamoto no Mochimitsu") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]]. ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''[[shōgun]]'' (the seventh of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]) at a young age, and was renamed "Minamoto no Koreyasu" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Fukakusa]]'s son [[Prince Hisaaki]] (the eighth ''[[shōgun]]'' of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]). Hisaaki's sons [[Prince Morikuni]] (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually [[Nijō Michihira]]'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''[[dainagon]]''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == See also == *[[History of Japan]] *[[Japanese clans]] *[[Japanese name]] *[[Minamoto (surname)]] *[[Taira clan]] *[[Genpei War|Genpei war]] *[[Fujiwara clan]] ==References== ==External links== {{commons category|Minamoto clan}} *[http://samurai-archives.com/HeianPeriod.html Heian Period: Minamoto Clan history] [[Category:Minamoto clan| ]] [[Category:Heian period]] [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]]

''(three [[Gentiana scabra|Japanese gentian flowers]] on five [[Bamboo|bamboo leaves]])'' |home province = [[Heian-kyō]] (Present: [[Kyoto]]) and various |parent house = [[File:Imperial Seal of Japan.svg|25px]] [[Imperial House of Japan]] |titles = [[Shogun]], [[Daimyo]], [[Kuge]], [[Kazoku]], and others |founder = Various; [[Minamoto no Makoto]] (first recorded) |final ruler = |current head = |founding year =c. 814 |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = {{Plainlist| * [[Saga Genji]] * [[Ninmyō Genji]] * [[Montoku Genji]] * [[Seiwa Genji]] * [[Yōzei Genji]] * [[Kōkō Genji]] * [[Uda Genji]] * [[Daigo Genji]] * Murakami Genji * [[Reizei Genji]] * [[Kazan Genji]] * [[Sanjō Genji]] * [[Go-Sanjō Genji]] * [[Go-Shirakawa Genji]] * [[Juntoku Genji]] * [[Go-Saga Genji]] * [[Go-Fusakusa Genji]] * [[Ōgimachi Genji]] * --- * '''Noble decendant clans:''' [[File:Japanese Crest Nitta hitotu Hiki.svg|15px]] [[Nitta clan|Nitta]], [[File:Ashikaga mon.svg|15px]] [[Ashikaga clan|Ashikaga]], [[File:Tokugawa family crest.svg|15px]] [[Matsudaira clan|Matsudaira]], [[File:Japanese Crest Takeda Hisi.svg|15px]] [[Takeda clan|Takeda]], [[File:Mitsubaaoi.svg|15px]] [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]], [[File:Japanese Crest Hosokawa Kuyou.svg|15px]] [[Hosokawa clan|Hosokawa]], [[File:五七桐に七葉根笹.png|15px]] [[Yamana clan|Yamana]], [[File:Japanese crest Imagawa Akadori.svg|15px]] [[Imagawa clan|Imagawa]], [[File:Kuyo.svg|15px]] [[Kanamaru clan|Kanamaru]], [[File:Japanese Crest Watanabe Hosi.svg|15px]] [[Watanabe|Watanabe]], [[File:Mizu-Iro Tokikikyo.png|15px]] [[Akechi clan|Akechi]], [[File:Tokikikyo.svg|15px]] [[Toki clan|Toki]], [[File:Ashikaga mon.svg|15px]] [[Shiba clan|Shiba]], and numberous others}} }} {{nihongo|'''Minamoto'''|源}} was one of the noble surnames bestowed by the [[Emperors of Japan]] upon members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|imperial family]] who were excluded from the line of succession and demoted into the ranks of the nobility from 1192 to 1333."...the Minamoto (1192-1333)" Warrior Rule in Japan, page 11. Cambridge University Press. The practice was most prevalent during the [[Heian period]] (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the [[Sengoku period]]. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the imperial dynasty, making both clans distant relatives. The Minamoto clan is also called the {{nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏}}, or less frequently, the {{nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家}}, using the [[on'yomi]] reading for Minamoto. The Minamoto were one of four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the [[Heian period]]—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the [[Tachibana clan (kuge)|Tachibana]]. == History == [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|right|[[Seiryō-ji]], a temple in [[Kyoto]], was once a villa of [[Minamoto no Tōru|Minamoto no Toru]] (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji]] [[File:Map-of-Japan-1183-Heian-Genpei-War.png|thumb|The domain of the Minamoto clan in Japan (1183) during the [[Genpei War]] ]] The first emperor to grant the surname Minamoto was [[Minamoto no Makoto]], seventh son of [[Emperor Saga]].Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press. The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the [[Seiwa Genji]], descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]] (897–961), a grandson of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka]] (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern [[Kyoto|Kyōto]]).{{rp|240–241}} Mitsunaka's eldest son, [[Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] (948–1021), became the protégé of [[Fujiwara no Michinaga]]; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of [[Taira no Tadatsune]] in 1032. Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including [[Minamoto no Tameyoshi]]. During the [[Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, [[Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]] and [[Emperor Toba|Toba]] and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the [[Genpei War]], Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192 he received the title ''[[shōgun]]'' and set up the first ''[[bakufu]]'' at [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]].{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} The later [[Ashikaga clan|Ashikaga]] (founders of the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]), [[Nitta family|Nitta]], and [[Takeda family|Takeda]] clans claim descent from the Seiwa Genji.{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA53|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|pages=53|language=en}}{{Cite book|last=Zöllner|first=Reinhard|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SwUvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=Die Ludowinger und die Takeda: Feudale Herrschaft in Thüringen und Kai no kuni|date=2018-02-15|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-7448-8682-6|pages=127|language=de}} The [[protagonist]] of the classical Japanese novel ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', [[Hikaru Genji]], was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The [[Genpei War]] is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last=Watson|first=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} [[File:Murasaki-Shikibu-composing-Genji-Monogatari.png|left|thumb|236x236px|[[Murasaki Shikibu]] composing ''Genji Monogatari'' ([[The Tale of Genji]])]] == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == [[File:Genealogy-of-the-Minamoto-Clan-Utagawa-Kuniyoshi.png|thumb|300px|Genealogy of the Minamoto clan, [[ukiyo-e]] by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]]] Even within royalty there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}} ("[having the] ability to advance", ''i.e.'', eligible to become the new Emperor), who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}} ("great" or "major"), who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the royal class (and therefore outranked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known [[Bhikkhu|monks]] of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favor of a [[dharma name]]). There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after the emperor from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few produced and no descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of [[Emperor Saga]]. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''[[Japanese name|uji]]'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, Makoto, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]] took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early [[Heian period]]. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. Clans such as the [[Watanabe]], [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji{{Cite book |url=http://www.daiichi-g.co.jp/kokugo/textbook/data/KA_316/KA_316_hs.pdf |title=高等学校 改訂版 古典Ａ 大鏡 源氏物語 諸家の文章 |publisher=株式会社第一学習社 |year=2018 |isbn=978-4-8040-1075-5 |edition=4th |pages=77-91 |language=ja}}. Noted Saga Genji and descendants include: * [[Minamoto no Makoto|Makoto]], seventh son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiromu|Hiromu]], eighth son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Hitoshi|Hitoshi]], grandson of Hiromu * [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Okoru|Okoru]], first son of Tokiwa * [[Minamoto no Sadamu|Sadamu]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Shitagō|Shitagō]], great-grandson of Sadamu * [[Minamoto no Hiroshi|Hiroshi]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]], son of the Emperor ** [[Anbō]] (secular name Minamoto no Shitagō), great-grandson of Tōru ** [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] (his official name was Minamoto no Tsuna, who resided at Watanabe in Settsu province, and took the name of the place), great-great-grandson of Tōru *** [[Matsuura Hisashi]], great-grandson of Tsuna ** [[Minamoto no Koreshige|Koreshige]], grandson of Tōru *** [[Minamoto no Mitsusue|Mitsusue]], great-great-grandson of Koreshige * [[Minamoto no Tsutomu|Tsutomu]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku|Hiraku]], son of the Emperor History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime|Kiyohime]], Sadahime, and Yoshihime), but few records concerning his daughters are known. ===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of [[Emperor Ninmyō]]. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru|Masaru]] and [[Minamoto no Hikaru|Hikaru]] were [[udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was Minamoto no Atsushi, adoptive father of the Saga Genji's [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] and father of the Seiwa Genji's [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Mitsunaka]]'s wife. ===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Montoku]]. Among them, [[Minamoto no Yoshiari|Yoshiari]] was a [[sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]]. ===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. The most numerous of them were those descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]], son of [[Prince Sadazumi]]. [[Minamoto no Yoshiie|Hachimantarō Yoshiie]] of the [[Kawachi Genji]] was a leader of a ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. His descendants set up the [[Kamakura shogunate]], making his a prestigious pedigree claimed by many ''buke'', particularly for the direct descendants in the [[Ashikaga clan]] (that set up the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]) and the rival [[Nitta clan]]. Centuries later, [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Yōzei]]. While [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]] is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by [[Hoshino Hisashi]]) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Yōzei rather than of Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behavior, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kōkō]]. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''[[busshi]]'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Uda]]. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], [[Minamoto no Masanobu|Masanobu]] and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu|Shigenobu]] became ''[[sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]'' the [[Sasaki clan]] of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Daigo]]. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]]. ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]''). ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa]] son [[Prince Mochihito|Mochihito-ō]] (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the [[Genpei War]], he was declassed (renamed "Minamoto no Mochimitsu") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]]. ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''[[shōgun]]'' (the seventh of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]) at a young age, and was renamed "Minamoto no Koreyasu" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Fukakusa]]'s son [[Prince Hisaaki]] (the eighth ''[[shōgun]]'' of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]). Hisaaki's sons [[Prince Morikuni]] (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually [[Nijō Michihira]]'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''[[dainagon]]''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == See also == *[[History of Japan]] *[[Japanese clans]] *[[Japanese name]] *[[Minamoto (surname)]] *[[Taira clan]] *[[Genpei War|Genpei war]] *[[Fujiwara clan]] ==References== ==External links== {{commons category|Minamoto clan}} *[http://samurai-archives.com/HeianPeriod.html Heian Period: Minamoto Clan history] [[Category:Minamoto clan| ]] [[Category:Heian period]] [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]]

Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including [[Minamoto no Tameyoshi]]. During the [[Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, [[Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]] and [[Emperor Toba|Toba]] and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the [[Genpei War]], Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192 he received the title ''[[shōgun]]'' and set up the first ''[[bakufu]]'' at [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]].{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} The later [[Ashikaga clan|Ashikaga]] (founders of the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]), [[Nitta family|Nitta]], and [[Takeda family|Takeda]] clans claim descent from the Seiwa Genji.{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA53|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|pages=53|language=en}}{{Cite book|last=Zöllner|first=Reinhard|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SwUvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=Die Ludowinger und die Takeda: Feudale Herrschaft in Thüringen und Kai no kuni|date=2018-02-15|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-7448-8682-6|pages=127|language=de}} The [[protagonist]] of the classical Japanese novel ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', [[Hikaru Genji]], was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The [[Genpei War]] is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last=Watson|first=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} [[File:Murasaki-Shikibu-composing-Genji-Monogatari.png|left|thumb|236x236px|[[Murasaki Shikibu]] composing ''Genji Monogatari'' ([[The Tale of Genji]])]] == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == [[File:Genealogy-of-the-Minamoto-Clan-Utagawa-Kuniyoshi.png|thumb|300px|Genealogy of the Minamoto clan, [[ukiyo-e]] by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]]] Even within royalty there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}} ("[having the] ability to advance", ''i.e.'', eligible to become the new Emperor), who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}} ("great" or "major"), who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the royal class (and therefore outranked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known [[Bhikkhu|monks]] of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favor of a [[dharma name]]). There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after the emperor from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few produced and no descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of [[Emperor Saga]]. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''[[Japanese name|uji]]'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, Makoto, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]] took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early [[Heian period]]. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. Clans such as the [[Watanabe]], [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji{{Cite book |url=http://www.daiichi-g.co.jp/kokugo/textbook/data/KA_316/KA_316_hs.pdf |title=高等学校 改訂版 古典Ａ 大鏡 源氏物語 諸家の文章 |publisher=株式会社第一学習社 |year=2018 |isbn=978-4-8040-1075-5 |edition=4th |pages=77-91 |language=ja}}. Noted Saga Genji and descendants include: * [[Minamoto no Makoto|Makoto]], seventh son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiromu|Hiromu]], eighth son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Hitoshi|Hitoshi]], grandson of Hiromu * [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Okoru|Okoru]], first son of Tokiwa * [[Minamoto no Sadamu|Sadamu]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Shitagō|Shitagō]], great-grandson of Sadamu * [[Minamoto no Hiroshi|Hiroshi]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Tōru|Tōru]], son of the Emperor ** [[Anbō]] (secular name Minamoto no Shitagō), great-grandson of Tōru ** [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] (his official name was Minamoto no Tsuna, who resided at Watanabe in Settsu province, and took the name of the place), great-great-grandson of Tōru *** [[Matsuura Hisashi]], great-grandson of Tsuna ** [[Minamoto no Koreshige|Koreshige]], grandson of Tōru *** [[Minamoto no Mitsusue|Mitsusue]], great-great-grandson of Koreshige * [[Minamoto no Tsutomu|Tsutomu]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku|Hiraku]], son of the Emperor History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime|Kiyohime]], Sadahime, and Yoshihime), but few records concerning his daughters are known. ===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of [[Emperor Ninmyō]]. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru|Masaru]] and [[Minamoto no Hikaru|Hikaru]] were [[udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was Minamoto no Atsushi, adoptive father of the Saga Genji's [[Watanabe no Tsuna]] and father of the Seiwa Genji's [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Mitsunaka]]'s wife. ===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Montoku]]. Among them, [[Minamoto no Yoshiari|Yoshiari]] was a [[sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]]. ===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. The most numerous of them were those descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]], son of [[Prince Sadazumi]]. [[Minamoto no Yoshiie|Hachimantarō Yoshiie]] of the [[Kawachi Genji]] was a leader of a ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]''. His descendants set up the [[Kamakura shogunate]], making his a prestigious pedigree claimed by many ''buke'', particularly for the direct descendants in the [[Ashikaga clan]] (that set up the [[Ashikaga shogunate]]) and the rival [[Nitta clan]]. Centuries later, [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Yōzei]]. While [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]] is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by [[Hoshino Hisashi]]) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Yōzei rather than of Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behavior, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kōkō]]. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''[[busshi]]'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Uda]]. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], [[Minamoto no Masanobu|Masanobu]] and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu|Shigenobu]] became ''[[sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]'' the [[Sasaki clan]] of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Daigo]]. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]]. ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]''). ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa]] son [[Prince Mochihito|Mochihito-ō]] (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the [[Genpei War]], he was declassed (renamed "Minamoto no Mochimitsu") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]]. ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''[[shōgun]]'' (the seventh of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]) at a young age, and was renamed "Minamoto no Koreyasu" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Fukakusa]]'s son [[Prince Hisaaki]] (the eighth ''[[shōgun]]'' of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]). Hisaaki's sons [[Prince Morikuni]] (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually [[Nijō Michihira]]'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''[[dainagon]]''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == See also == *[[History of Japan]] *[[Japanese clans]] *[[Japanese name]] *[[Minamoto (surname)]] *[[Taira clan]] *[[Genpei War|Genpei war]] *[[Fujiwara clan]] ==References== ==External links== {{commons category|Minamoto clan}} *[http://samurai-archives.com/HeianPeriod.html Heian Period: Minamoto Clan history] [[Category:Minamoto clan| ]] [[Category:Heian period]] [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]]

Cambridge University Press. The practice was most prevalent during the [[Heian period]] (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the [[Sengoku period]]. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the imperial dynasty, making both clans distant relatives. The Minamoto clan is also called the {{nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏}}, or less frequently, the {{nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家}}, using the [[on'yomi]] reading for Minamoto. The Minamoto were one of four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the [[Heian period]]—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the [[Tachibana clan (kuge)|Tachibana]]. == History == [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|[[Seiryō-ji]], a temple in [[Kyoto]], was once a villa of [[Minamoto no Tōru]] (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji]] [[File:Map-of-Japan-1183-Heian-Genpei-War.png|thumb|The domain of the Minamoto clan in Japan (1183) during the [[Genpei War]] ]] The first emperor to grant the surname Minamoto was [[Minamoto no Makoto]], seventh son of [[Emperor Saga]].Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press. The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the [[Seiwa Genji]], descended from [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]] (897–961), a grandson of [[Emperor Seiwa]]. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. [[Minamoto no Mitsunaka]] (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern [[Kyoto|Kyōto]]).{{rp|240–241}} Mitsunaka's eldest son, [[Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] (948–1021), became the protégé of [[Fujiwara no Michinaga]]; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of [[Taira no Tadatsune]] in 1032. Centuries later, [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Yōzei]]. While [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto|Tsunemoto]] is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by [[Hoshino Hisashi]]) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Yōzei rather than of Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behavior, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kōkō]]. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''[[busshi]]'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Uda]]. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], [[Minamoto no Masanobu|Masanobu]] and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu|Shigenobu]] became ''[[sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''[[buke (Japan)|buke]]'' the [[Sasaki clan]] of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Daigo]]. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira|Takaakira]] became a ''[[sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson [[Minamoto no Hiromasa|Hiromasa]] was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Murakami]]. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the [[Ashikaga clan]] took it during the [[Muromachi period]], the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Reizei]]. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Kazan]]. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Jingi-kan]] for centuries, responsible for the centralized aspects of [[Shinto]]. ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue|Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the [[Ministry of the Imperial Household]] was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Sanjō]]'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito|Arihito]] was a ''[[sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''[[Genpei Jōsuiki]]''). ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Shirakawa]] son [[Prince Mochihito|Mochihito-ō]] (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the [[Genpei War]], he was declassed (renamed "Minamoto no Mochimitsu") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Juntoku]]'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[sadaijin]]'' with the help of [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]]. ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of [[Emperor Go-Saga]]'s grandson [[Prince Koreyasu]]. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''[[shōgun]]'' (the seventh of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]) at a young age, and was renamed "Minamoto no Koreyasu" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of [[Emperor Go-Fukakusa]]'s son [[Prince Hisaaki]] (the eighth ''[[shōgun]]'' of the [[Kamakura shogunate]]). Hisaaki's sons [[Prince Morikuni]] (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually [[Nijō Michihira]]'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''[[dainagon]]''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of [[Emperor Ōgimachi]]. At first they were ''[[Buke (Japan)|buke]]'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == See also == *[[History of Japan]] *[[Japanese clans]] *[[Japanese name]] *[[Minamoto (surname)]] *[[Taira clan]] *[[Genpei War|Genpei war]] *[[Fujiwara clan]] ==References== ==External links== {{commons category|Minamoto clan}} *[http://samurai-archives.com/HeianPeriod.html Heian Period: Minamoto Clan history] [[Category:Minamoto clan| ]] [[Category:Heian period]] [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]]
