the Minamoto clan
''(three {{ill|Gentiana scabra|en|Gentiana scabra|WD=Q926053|lt=Japanese gentian flowers}} on five {{ill|Bamboo|en|Bamboo|WD=Q670887|lt=bamboo leaves}})'' |home province = {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō}} (Modern [[:en:Kyōto|Kyōto]]) |parent house = {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=Imperial House of Japan}}
({{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}) |titles = {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}, [[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]], [[Kuge]], {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|WD=Q1157586|lt=Daijō-daijin}}, {{ill|Minister of the Left|en|Minister of the Left|WD=Q949008|lt=Sadaijin}}, {{ill|Minister of the Right|en|Minister of the Right|WD=Q1351174|lt=Udaijin}}, [[Kazoku]], and others |founder = {{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}} (first recorded) |final ruler = |current head = |founding year =May {{ill|814|en|814|WD=Q23447|lt=814}} ({{Age|1 May 814}} years ago) |dissolution = |ruled until =still extant |cadet branches = {{Plain list| * [[Saga Genji]] * [[Ninmyō Genji]] * [[Montoku Genji]] * {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} * [[Yōzei Genji]] * [[Kōkō Genji]] * {{ill|Uda Genji|en|Uda Genji|WD=Q4846201|lt=Uda Genji}} * [[Daigo Genji]] * Murakami Genji * [[Reizei Genji]] * [[Kazan Genji]] * [[Sanjō Genji]] * [[Go-Sanjō Genji]] * [[Go-Shirakawa Genji]] * [[Juntoku Genji]] * [[Go-Saga Genji]] * [[Go-Fusakusa Genji]] * [[Ōgimachi Genji]] }} }} {{Nihongo|'''Minamoto'''|源}} was a {{ill|Aristocracy (class)|en|Aristocracy (class)|WD=Q2478141|lt=noble}} surname bestowed by the [[:en:Emperors of Japan|Emperors of Japan]] upon members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial family}} who were excluded from the {{ill|List of emperors of Japan|en|List of emperors of Japan|WD=Q188210|lt=line of succession}} and demoted into the Ranks of [[:en:Japanese nobility|the nobility]] since 814."...the Minamoto (1192-1333)". ''Warrior Rule in Japan'', page 11. Cambridge University Press.{{Cite book |last=井上 |first=辰雄 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_panuAAACAAJ |title=嵯峨天皇と文人官僚 |publisher=塙書房 |year=2011 |isbn=9784827312409 |location=Japan |pages=305–306 |language=ja}} Several noble lines were bestowed the surname, the most notable of which was the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}, whose descendants established the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura}} and {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga}} {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=shogunates}} following the Heian era. The Minamoto was one of the four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian}} period in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the {{ill|Tachibana clan (kuge)|en|Tachibana clan (kuge)|WD=Q1500519|lt=Tachibana}}.{{Cite encyclopedia |last=Gibney |first=FRank |year=1984 |title=Shisei: 'Genji' |encyclopedia=Britannica International Encyclopedia |publisher=TBS-Britannica |oclc=47462068}}{{Cite book |last=Frédéric |first=Louis |year=2002 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=9780674017535 |pages=439–452 |language=en}} In the late Heian period, Minamoto rivalry with the Taira culminated in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} (1180–1185 AD). The Minamoto emerged victorious and established Japan's first {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=shogunate}} in {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} under [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], who appointed himself as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' in 1192, ushering in the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} (1192–1333 AD) of Japanese history. The name "Genpei" comes from {{ill|On'yomi|en|On'yomi|WD=Q718498|lt=alternate readings}} of the ''{{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=Kanji}}'' "Minamoto" (源 ''Gen'') and "Taira" (平 ''Hei''). The Kamakura Shogunate was overthrown by {{ill|Emperor Go-Daigo|en|Emperor Go-Daigo|WD=Q313942|lt=Emperor Go-Daigo}} in the [[Kenmu Restoration]] of 1333. Three years later the Kenmu government would then itself be overthrown by the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}}, descendants of the Seiwa Genji who established the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} (1333 to 1573). The Minamoto clan is also called the {{Nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏|4="Minamoto clan"}}, or less frequently, the {{Nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家|4="House of Minamoto"}}, using the {{ill|On'yomi|en|On'yomi|WD=Q718498|lt=On'yomi}} readings of {{nihongo|''gen''|源}} for "Minamoto", while {{Nihongo|''shi'' or ''ji''|氏}} means "[[Uji (clan)|clan]]", and {{Nihongo|''ke''|家}} is used as a suffix for "{{ill|Extended family|en|Extended family|WD=Q721790|lt=Extended family}}".{{Cite book |last=Lebra |first=Takie Sugiyama |year=1995 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xa0wDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA72 |title=Above the Clouds: Status Culture of the Modern Japanese Nobility |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=9780520076020 |language=en}} == History == The [[:en:Emperors of Japan|Emperors of Japan]] bestowed noble surnames upon members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial family}} who were excluded from the {{ill|List of emperors of Japan|en|List of emperors of Japan|WD=Q188210|lt=line of succession}} and demoted into the Ranks of [[:en:Japanese nobility|the nobility]]. In May 814, the first {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=emperor}} to grant the surname "Minamoto" was {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}, to his seventh son—{{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}}, in [[:en:Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto}}).Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press.{{Cite book |last=倉本 |first=一宏 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3FClzAEACAAJ |title=公家源氏: 王権を支えた名族 |publisher=中央公論新社 |date=2019-12-18 |isbn=9784121025739 |location=Japan |pages=18 |language=ja}}{{rp|18}} The practice was most prevalent during the Heian period (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial dynasty}}, making both clans distant relatives.{{Cite book |last=Kuehn |first=John T. |title=A military history of Japan: from the age of the Samurai to the 21st century |date=2014 |publisher=Praeger |isbn=978-1-4408-0394-9 |location=Santa Barbara, Calif. |pages=36}} [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Seiryō-ji|en|Seiryō-ji|WD=Q534101|lt=Seiryō-ji}}, a temple in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, was once a villa of {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Minamoto no Tōru}} (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji|left]]The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}, descended from {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} (897–961), a grandson of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa}}. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|en|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|WD=Q2531241|lt=Minamoto no Mitsunaka}} (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[:en:Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto}}).{{rp|240–241}}Mitsunaka's eldest son, {{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} (948–1021), became the protégé of {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of {{ill|Taira no Tadatsune|en|Taira no Tadatsune|WD=Q1105844|lt=Taira no Tadatsune}} in 1032. Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} [[File:Emperor Saga.jpg|left|thumb|399x399px|{{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}} (786 – 842)]] The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[:en:Hōgen Rebellion|Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including {{ill|Minamoto no Tameyoshi|en|Minamoto no Tameyoshi|WD=Q1381638|lt=Minamoto no Tameyoshi}}. During the [[:en:Heiji Disturbance|Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}}, died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Go-Shirakawa}} and {{ill|Emperor Toba|en|Emperor Toba|WD=Q349284|lt=Toba}} and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}}, Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192, he received the title ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' and set up the first ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' in the history of Japan at {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}—{{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}.{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} [[File:Minamoto no Makoto.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}} (810 – 868)]] The later {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga}} (founders of the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} of {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}), [[:en:Nitta family|Nitta]], [[:en:Takeda family|Takeda]], and [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]] (founders of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] of {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}) clans claim descents from the Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji branch).{{Cite book|last1=Frederic|first1=Louis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA53|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|pages=53|language=en}}{{Cite book|last=Zöllner|first=Reinhard|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SwUvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=Die Ludowinger und die Takeda: Feudale Herrschaft in Thüringen und Kai no kuni|date=2018-02-15|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-7448-8682-6|pages=127|language=de}}[[File:Map-of-Japan-1183-Heian-Genpei-War.png|thumb|The domain of the Minamoto clan in Japan (1183) during the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} ]] The {{ill|protagonist|en|protagonist|WD=Q215972|lt=protagonist}} of the classical Japanese novel ''{{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji}} (The Tale of Minamoto clan)—''{{ill|Hikaru Genji|en|Hikaru Genji|WD=Q997646|lt=Hikaru Genji}}, was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''{{ill|The Tale of the Heike|en|The Tale of the Heike|WD=Q830740|lt=The Tale of the Heike}}'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last1=Watson|first1=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == Even within {{ill|Royal family|en|Royal family|WD=Q2006518|lt=royalty}} there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}}, who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}}, who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=royal class}} (and therefore outRanked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social Rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. [[File:Old silver coin with family crest of Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji), Edo period.png|left|thumb|291x291px|{{ill|Silver coin|en|Silver coin|WD=Q610038|lt=Old silver coin}} with [[Mon (emblem)|mon]](emblem) of the Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji), found in {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}]] Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=monks}} of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favour of a {{ill|Dharma name|en|Dharma name|WD=Q1543672|lt=Dharma name}}). [[File:Kabuto attached with family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) 源氏家紋の笹竜胆付ける兜.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kabuto|en|Kabuto|WD=Q1720878|lt=Kabuto}} attached with [[Mon (emblem)|Mon]] (emblem) of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou)]] The Minamoto is the ancestor and parent clan of many notable descendant clans, some of which are {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga}}, [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]], {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira}}, {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta}}, [[Takeda clan|Takeda]], {{ill|Shimazu clan|en|Shimazu clan|WD=Q1061406|lt=Shimazu}}, {{ill|Sasaki clan|en|Sasaki clan|WD=Q1028587|lt=Sasaki}}, {{ill|Akamatsu clan|en|Akamatsu clan|WD=Q2659667|lt=Akamatsu}}, [[Kitabatake clan|Kitabatake]], Tada, {{ill|Ōta clan|en|Ōta clan|WD=Q1391922|lt=Ota}}, [[Toki clan|Toki]], {{ill|Yamana clan|en|Yamana clan|WD=Q2975406|lt=Yamana}}, {{ill|Satomi clan|en|Satomi clan|WD=Q2975367|lt=Satomi}}, {{ill|Hosokawa clan|en|Hosokawa clan|WD=Q2736120|lt=Hosokawa}}, {{ill|Satake clan|en|Satake clan|WD=Q2975363|lt=Satake}}, Yamamoto, Hemi, {{ill|Ogasawara clan|en|Ogasawara clan|WD=Q2975340|lt=Ogasawara}}, {{ill|Yasuda clan|en|Yasuda clan|WD=Q8049951|lt=Yasuda}}, Takenouchi, Hiraga, [[Imagawa clan|Imagawa]], {{ill|Miyake clan|en|Miyake clan|WD=Q2975320|lt=Miyake}}, etc.{{Cite book |last=Papinot |first=Jacques Edmond Joseph |url=http://www.unterstein.net/Toyoashihara-no-Chiaki-Nagaioaki-no-Mitsuho-no-Kuni/NobiliaireJapon.pdf |title=Nobiliaire du Japon |publisher=Oliver Rost; Stefan Unterstein |year=1906 |location=Dortmund; München |pages=3–73 |language=fr}} There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=the emperor}} from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few did not produce descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''{{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=uji}}'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, {{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Makoto}}, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Tōru}} took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}''. Clans such as the {{ill|Watanabe|en|Watanabe|WD=Q10983405|lt=Watanabe}}, [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji.{{Cite book |url=http://www.daiichi-g.co.jp/kokugo/textbook/data/KA_316/KA_316_hs.pdf |title=高等学校 改訂版 古典Ａ 大鏡 源氏物語 諸家の文章 |publisher=株式会社第一学習社 |year=2018 |isbn=978-4-8040-1075-5 |edition=4th |pages=43–56 |language=ja}}[[File:Murasaki-Shikibu-composing-Genji-Monogatari.png|thumb|279x279px|{{ill|Murasaki Shikibu|en|Murasaki Shikibu|WD=Q81731|lt=Murasaki Shikibu}} composing ''Genji Monogatari'' ({{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji}})]] Noted Saga Genji and descendants include: * {{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}}, seventh son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiromu]], eighth son of the Emperor ** {{ill|Minamoto no Hitoshi|en|Minamoto no Hitoshi|WD=Q2364746|lt=Minamoto no Hitoshi}}, grandson of Hiromu * [[Minamoto no Tokiwa]], son of the Emperor ** [[Minamoto no Okoru]], first son of Tokiwa * [[Minamoto no Sadamu]], son of the Emperor ** {{ill|Minamoto no Shitagō|en|Minamoto no Shitagō|WD=Q1559382|lt=Minamoto no Shitagō}}, great-grandson of Sadamu * [[Minamoto no Hiroshi]], son of the Emperor * {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Minamoto no Tōru}}, son of the Emperor[[File:Minamoto no Yoritomo.jpg|thumb|Portrait of [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199) in 1179, by {{ill|Fujiwara no Takanobu|en|Fujiwara no Takanobu|WD=Q2245281|lt=Fujiwara no Takanobu}}|left]] ** [[:en:Anbō|Minamoto no Anbō]] (secular name Minamoto no Shitagō), great-grandson of Tōru ** {{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Watanabe no Tsuna}} (his official name was {{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Minamoto no Tsuna}}, who resided at Watanabe in Settsu province, and took the name of the place), great-great-grandson of Tōru *** [[Matsuura Hisashi]], great-grandson of Tsuna ** [[Minamoto no Koreshige]], grandson of Tōru *** [[Minamoto no Mitsusue]], great-great-grandson of Koreshige * [[Minamoto no Tsutomu]], son of the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku]], son of the Emperor History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime]], [[Minamoto no Sadahime]], and [[Minamoto no Yoshihime]]), but few records concerning his daughters are known.[[File:Kuniyoshi Imperial Bodyguard Fighting with a Demon.jpg|thumb|285x285px|{{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Minamoto no Tsuna}} cutting the arm off the demon Ibaraki]] ===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Ninmyō|en|Emperor Ninmyō|WD=Q349271|lt=Emperor Ninmyō}}. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru]] and [[:en:Minamoto no Hikaru|Minamoto no Hikaru]] were [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was [[Minamoto no Atsushi]], adoptive father of the Saga Genji's {{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Watanabe no Tsuna}} and father of the Seiwa Genji's {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|en|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|WD=Q2531241|lt=Minamoto no Mitsunaka}}'s wife. ===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Montoku|en|Emperor Montoku|WD=Q357225|lt=Emperor Montoku}}. Among them, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiari|en|Minamoto no Yoshiari|WD=Q11564289|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiari}} was a [[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]]. ===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa}}. The most numerous of them were those descended from {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}}, son of [[Prince Sadazumi]]. {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Hachimantarō Yoshiie}} of the {{ill|Kawachi Genji|en|Kawachi Genji|WD=Q5360652|lt=Kawachi Genji}} was a leader of a ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}''. His descendants set up the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, making his a prestigious pedigree claimed by many ''buke'', particularly for the direct descendants in the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}} (that set up the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}}) and the rival {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta clan}}. Centuries later, {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune.jpg|left|thumb|Portrait of [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] (1159–1189)]] ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Yōzei|en|Emperor Yōzei|WD=Q349280|lt=Emperor Yōzei}}. While {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by {{ill|Hoshino Hisashi|en|Hoshino Hisashi|WD=Q724526|lt=Hoshino Hisashi}}) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Emperor Yōzei rather than of Emperor Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behaviour, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== [[File:Minamoto no Tsunemoto.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} (894–961)]] These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Kōkō|en|Emperor Kōkō|WD=Q440518|lt=Emperor Kōkō}}. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''{{ill|Busshi|en|Busshi|WD=Q2928765|lt=Busshi}}'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Uda|en|Emperor Uda|WD=Q349267|lt=Emperor Uda}}. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], {{ill|Minamoto no Masanobu|en|Minamoto no Masanobu|WD=Q3314711|lt=Minamoto no Masanobu}} and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu]] became ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}'' the {{ill|Sasaki clan|en|Sasaki clan|WD=Q1028587|lt=Sasaki clan}} of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. [[File:Minamoto Yorimitsu.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} (948–1021)]] ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Daigo|en|Emperor Daigo|WD=Q329753|lt=Emperor Daigo}}. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira]] became a ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson {{ill|Minamoto no Hiromasa|en|Minamoto no Hiromasa|WD=Q3276201|lt=Minamoto no Hiromasa}} was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Murakami|en|Emperor Murakami|WD=Q374015|lt=Emperor Murakami}}. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}} took it during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}, the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. [[File:Painting of Minamoto no Sanetomo by Yashima Gakutei, 1825.jpg|thumb|220x220px|Painting of [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]] (1192–1219) – {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura}} {{ill|Minister of the Right|en|Minister of the Right|WD=Q1351174|lt=Udaijin}}]] ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Reizei|en|Emperor Reizei|WD=Q374125|lt=Emperor Reizei}}. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Kazan}}. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Department of Divinities]] for centuries, responsible for the centralised aspects of [[Shinto]]. [[File:Minamoto no Yoshinaka.jpg|left|thumb|A portrait of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|en|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|WD=Q1139202|lt=Minamoto no Yoshinaka}} (1154–1184)]] ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Sanjō|en|Emperor Sanjō|WD=Q357231|lt=Emperor Sanjō}}'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the {{ill|Ministry of the Imperial Household|en|Ministry of the Imperial Household|WD=Q8193428|lt=Ministry of the Imperial Household}} was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Go-Sanjō|en|Emperor Go-Sanjō|WD=Q45844|lt=Emperor Go-Sanjō}}'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito]] was a ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[:en:Tale of the Heike|Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''{{ill|Genpei Jōsuiki|en|Genpei Jōsuiki|WD=Q3020148|lt=Genpei Jōsuiki}}''). [[File:Minamoto no Yoriie (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Minamoto no Yoriie]] (1182–1204)]] ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}} son {{ill|Prince Mochihito|en|Prince Mochihito|WD=Q1941666|lt=Mochihito-ō}} (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}}, he was declassed (renamed "[[Minamoto no Mochimitsu]]") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Juntoku|en|Emperor Juntoku|WD=Q357249|lt=Emperor Juntoku}}'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]'' with the help of {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|en|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|WD=Q248381|lt=Ashikaga Yoshimitsu}}. [[File:Minamoto Yorinobu.jpg|left|thumb|356x356px|[[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048)]] ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of {{ill|Emperor Go-Saga|en|Emperor Go-Saga|WD=Q349259|lt=Emperor Go-Saga}}'s grandson {{ill|Prince Koreyasu|en|Prince Koreyasu|WD=Q586532|lt=Prince Koreyasu}}. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' (the seventh of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}) at a young age, and was renamed "{{ill|Prince Koreyasu|en|Prince Koreyasu|WD=Q586532|lt=Minamoto no Koreyasu}}" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. [[File:A wooden signboard with a family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) 源氏家紋の丸に笹竜胆付ける木製看板.jpg|thumb|A wooden signboard with a family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) ]] ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|en|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|WD=Q349246|lt=Emperor Go-Fukakusa}}'s son {{ill|Prince Hisaaki|en|Prince Hisaaki|WD=Q715826|lt=Prince Hisaaki}} (the eighth ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}). Hisaaki's sons {{ill|Prince Morikuni|en|Prince Morikuni|WD=Q552852|lt=Prince Morikuni}} (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually {{ill|Nijō Michihira|en|Nijō Michihira|WD=Q3341478|lt=Nijō Michihira}}'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''{{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon}}''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of {{ill|Emperor Ōgimachi|en|Emperor Ōgimachi|WD=Q334076|lt=Emperor Ōgimachi}}. At first they were ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == Legacy == === Historical periods and cities founding === [[File:Kamakura - Grand Bouddha.jpg|thumb|The statue of [[Amitābha|Amida Buddha]] at {{ill|Kōtoku-in|en|Kōtoku-in|WD=Q672056|lt=Kōtoku-in}}, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}]] * {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} and {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura city}}, which were established and founded by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]''—''the first ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' of Japan. * {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} was founded by ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|en|Ashikaga Takauji|WD=Q297107|lt=Ashikaga Takauji}}''—''a direct descendant of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiyasu|en|Minamoto no Yoshiyasu|WD=Q6863161|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiyasu}} (also known as ''Ashikaga Yoshiyasu''). * {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} was founded by ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}''—''who claimed to be a descendant of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshishige|en|Minamoto no Yoshishige|WD=Q732097|lt=Minamoto no Yoshishige}} (also known as ''Nitta Yoshishige''). === Shinto shrines founding === [[File:Rokusonnnou-Jinja shinmon.JPG|thumb|''Shinmon'' of {{ill|Rokusonnō Shrine|en|Rokusonnō Shrine|WD=Q11392320|lt=Rokusonnō Shrine}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}]] * {{Nihongo|{{ill|Three Genji Shrines|en|Three Genji Shrines|WD=Q7797495|lt=Three Genji Shrines}}|源氏三神社|Genji San Jinja}} - A group of Shinto shrines connected closedly with the members of {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} branch of the Minamoto clan. ** {{ill|Rokusonnō Shrine|en|Rokusonnō Shrine|WD=Q11392320|lt=Rokusonnō Shrine}}, {{ill|Minami-ku, Kyoto|en|Minami-ku, Kyoto|WD=Q1154649|lt=Minami-ku}}, Kyoto, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture}} ** [[:en:Tada Jinja|Tada Jinja]], {{ill|Kawanishi, Hyōgo|en|Kawanishi, Hyōgo|WD=Q609350|lt=Kawanishi}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}} ** {{ill|Tsuboi Hachimangū|en|Tsuboi Hachimangū|WD=Q11429677|lt=Tsuboi Hachimangū}}, [[:en:Habikino, Osaka|Habikino]], {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture}} *[[:ja:沙沙貴神社|Sasaki Shrine]] {{Nihongo|2=沙沙貴神社}} - a Shinto shrine connected closely with the members of {{ill|Uda Genji|en|Uda Genji|WD=Q4846201|lt=Uda Genji}} branch of the Minamoto clan. === Literature and arts === [[File:Seated Portrait of Minamoto no Yoritomo (Presumed) 1.jpg|left|thumb|220x220px|Seated Portrait of [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] - {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}} in {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|en|Tokyo National Museum|WD=Q653433|lt=Tokyo National Museum}}]] * {{Nihongo|{{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji}}|源氏物語|Genji monogatari|The Tale of the Minamoto clan}} by {{ill|Murasaki Shikibu|en|Murasaki Shikibu|WD=Q81731|lt=Murasaki Shikibu}}, an important 11th-century classical Japanese novel.[[File:Genji monogatari (ch. 34).jpg|thumb|Genji monogatari]] * {{Nihongo|{{ill|The Tale of the Heike|en|The Tale of the Heike|WD=Q830740|lt=The Tale of the Heike}}|平家物語|Heike Monogatari|The Tale of house of Taira}}'','' a 14th-century {{ill|Epic poetry|en|Epic poetry|WD=Q37484|lt=Epic poetry}} compiled of the struggle between the Minamoto clan and the [[Taira clan]] for control of Japan at the end of the 12th century in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} (1180–1185). == See also == *{{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=History of Japan}} *[[Japanese clans]] *{{ill|Minamoto (surname)|en|Minamoto ''Warrior Rule in Japan'', page 11. Cambridge University Press.{{Cite book |last=井上 |first=辰雄 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_panuAAACAAJ |title=嵯峨天皇と文人官僚 |publisher=塙書房 |year=2011 |isbn=9784827312409 |location=Japan |pages=305–306 |language=ja}} Several noble lines were bestowed the surname, the most notable of which was the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}, whose descendants established the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura}} and {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga}} {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=shogunates}} following the Heian era. The Minamoto was one of the four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian}} period in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the {{ill|Tachibana clan (kuge)|en|Tachibana clan (kuge)|WD=Q1500519|lt=Tachibana}}.{{Cite encyclopedia |last=Gibney |first=FRank |year=1984 |title=Shisei: 'Genji' |encyclopedia=Britannica International Encyclopedia |publisher=TBS-Britannica |oclc=47462068}}{{Cite book |last=Frédéric |first=Louis |year=2002 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=9780674017535 |pages=439–452 |language=en}} In the late Heian period, Minamoto rivalry with the Taira culminated in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} (1180–1185 AD). The Minamoto emerged victorious and established Japan's first {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=shogunate}} in {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} under [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], who appointed himself as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' in 1192, ushering in the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} (1192–1333 AD) of Japanese history. The name "Genpei" comes from {{ill|On'yomi|en|On'yomi|WD=Q718498|lt=alternate readings}} of the ''{{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=Kanji}}'' "Minamoto" (源 ''Gen'') and "Taira" (平 ''Hei''). The Kamakura Shogunate was overthrown by {{ill|Emperor Go-Daigo|en|Emperor Go-Daigo|WD=Q313942|lt=Emperor Go-Daigo}} in the [[Kenmu Restoration]] of 1333. Three years later the Kenmu government would then itself be overthrown by the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}}, descendants of the Seiwa Genji who established the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} (1333 to 1573). The Minamoto clan is also called the {{Nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏|4="Minamoto clan"}}, or less frequently, the {{Nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家|4="House of Minamoto"}}, using the {{ill|On'yomi|en|On'yomi|WD=Q718498|lt=On'yomi}} readings of {{nihongo|''gen''|源}} for "Minamoto", while {{Nihongo|''shi'' or ''ji''|氏}} means "[[Uji (clan)|clan]]", and {{Nihongo|''ke''|家}} is used as a suffix for "{{ill|Extended family|en|Extended family|WD=Q721790|lt=Extended family}}".{{Cite book |last=Lebra |first=Takie Sugiyama |year=1995 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xa0wDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA72 |title=Above the Clouds: Status Culture of the Modern Japanese Nobility |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=9780520076020 |language=en}} == History == The [[:en:Emperors of Japan|Emperors of Japan]] bestowed noble surnames upon members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial family}} who were excluded from the {{ill|List of emperors of Japan|en|List of emperors of Japan|WD=Q188210|lt=line of succession}} and demoted into the Ranks of [[:en:Japanese nobility|the nobility]]. In May 814, the first {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=emperor}} to grant the surname "Minamoto" was {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}, to his seventh son—{{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}}, in [[:en:Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto}}).Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press.{{Cite book |last=倉本 |first=一宏 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3FClzAEACAAJ |title=公家源氏: 王権を支えた名族 |publisher=中央公論新社 |date=2019-12-18 |isbn=9784121025739 |location=Japan |pages=18 |language=ja}}{{rp|18}} The practice was most prevalent during the Heian period (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial dynasty}}, making both clans distant relatives.{{Cite book |last=Kuehn |first=John T. |title=A military history of Japan: from the age of the Samurai to the 21st century |date=2014 |publisher=Praeger |isbn=978-1-4408-0394-9 |location=Santa Barbara, Calif. |pages=36}} [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Seiryō-ji|en|Seiryō-ji|WD=Q534101|lt=Seiryō-ji}}, a temple in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, was once a villa of {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Minamoto no Tōru}} (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji|left]]The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}, descended from {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} (897–961), a grandson of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa}}. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|en|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|WD=Q2531241|lt=Minamoto no Mitsunaka}} (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[:en:Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto}}).{{rp|240–241}}Mitsunaka's eldest son, {{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} (948–1021), became the protégé of {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of {{ill|Taira no Tadatsune|en|Taira no Tadatsune|WD=Q1105844|lt=Taira no Tadatsune}} in 1032. Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} [[File:Emperor Saga.jpg|left|thumb|399x399px|{{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}} (786 – 842)]] The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[:en:Hōgen Rebellion|Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including {{ill|Minamoto no Tameyoshi|en|Minamoto no Tameyoshi|WD=Q1381638|lt=Minamoto no Tameyoshi}}. During the [[:en:Heiji Disturbance|Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}}, died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Go-Shirakawa}} and {{ill|Emperor Toba|en|Emperor Toba|WD=Q349284|lt=Toba}} and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}}, Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192, he received the title ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' and set up the first ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' in the history of Japan at {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}—{{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}.{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} [[File:Minamoto no Makoto.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}} (810 – 868)]] The later {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga}} (founders of the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} of {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}), [[:en:Nitta family|Nitta]], [[:en:Takeda family|Takeda]], and [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]] (founders of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] of {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}) clans claim descents from the during the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} ]] The {{ill|protagonist|en|protagonist|WD=Q215972|lt=protagonist}} of the classical Japanese novel ''{{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji}} (The Tale of Minamoto clan)—''{{ill|Hikaru Genji|en|Hikaru Genji|WD=Q997646|lt=Hikaru Genji}}, was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''{{ill|The Tale of the Heike|en|The Tale of the Heike|WD=Q830740|lt=The Tale of the Heike}}'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last1=Watson|first1=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == Even within {{ill|Royal family|en|Royal family|WD=Q2006518|lt=royalty}} there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}}, who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}}, who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=royal class}} (and therefore outRanked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social Rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. [[File:Old silver coin with family crest of Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji), Edo period.png|left|thumb|291x291px|{{ill|Silver coin|en|Silver coin|WD=Q610038|lt=Old silver coin}} with [[Mon (emblem)|mon]](emblem) of the Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji), found in {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}]] Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=monks}} of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favour of a {{ill|Dharma name|en|Dharma name|WD=Q1543672|lt=Dharma name}}). [[File:Kabuto attached with family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) 源氏家紋の笹竜胆付ける兜.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kabuto|en|Kabuto|WD=Q1720878|lt=Kabuto}} attached with [[Mon (emblem)|Mon]] (emblem) of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou)]] The Minamoto is the ancestor and parent clan of many notable descendant clans, some of which are {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga}}, [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]], {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira}}, {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta}}, [[Takeda clan|Takeda]], {{ill|Shimazu clan|en|Shimazu clan|WD=Q1061406|lt=Shimazu}}, {{ill|Sasaki clan|en|Sasaki clan|WD=Q1028587|lt=Sasaki}}, {{ill|Akamatsu clan|en|Akamatsu clan|WD=Q2659667|lt=Akamatsu}}, [[Kitabatake clan|Kitabatake]], Tada, {{ill|Ōta clan|en|Ōta clan|WD=Q1391922|lt=Ota}}, [[Toki clan|Toki]], {{ill|Yamana clan|en|Yamana clan|WD=Q2975406|lt=Yamana}}, {{ill|Satomi clan|en|Satomi clan|WD=Q2975367|lt=Satomi}}, {{ill|Hosokawa clan|en|Hosokawa clan|WD=Q2736120|lt=Hosokawa}}, {{ill|Satake clan|en|Satake clan|WD=Q2975363|lt=Satake}}, Yamamoto, Hemi, {{ill|Ogasawara clan|en|Ogasawara clan|WD=Q2975340|lt=Ogasawara}}, {{ill|Yasuda clan|en|Yasuda clan|WD=Q8049951|lt=Yasuda}}, Takenouchi, Hiraga, [[Imagawa clan|Imagawa]], {{ill|Miyake clan|en|Miyake clan|WD=Q2975320|lt=Miyake}}, etc.{{Cite book |last=Papinot |first=Jacques Edmond Joseph |url=http://www.unterstein.net/Toyoashihara-no-Chiaki-Nagaioaki-no-Mitsuho-no-Kuni/NobiliaireJapon.pdf |title=Nobiliaire du Japon |publisher=Oliver Rost; Stefan Unterstein |year=1906 |location=Dortmund; München |pages=3–73 |language=fr}} There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=the emperor}} from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few did not produce descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''{{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=uji}}'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, {{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Makoto}}, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Tōru}} took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}''. Clans such as the {{ill|Watanabe|en|Watanabe|WD=Q10983405|lt=Watanabe}}, [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji.{{Cite book the Emperor * [[Minamoto no Hiraku]], son of the Emperor History records indicate that at least three of Emperor Saga's daughters were also made Minamoto ([[Minamoto no Kiyohime]], [[Minamoto no Sadahime]], and [[Minamoto no Yoshihime]]), but few records concerning his daughters are known.[[File:Kuniyoshi Imperial Bodyguard Fighting with a Demon.jpg|thumb|285x285px|{{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Minamoto no Tsuna}} cutting the arm off the demon Ibaraki]] ===Ninmyō Genji=== They were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Ninmyō|en|Emperor Ninmyō|WD=Q349271|lt=Emperor Ninmyō}}. His sons [[Minamoto no Masaru]] and [[:en:Minamoto no Hikaru|Minamoto no Hikaru]] were [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]. Among Hikaru's descendants was [[Minamoto no Atsushi]], adoptive father of the Saga Genji's {{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Watanabe no Tsuna}} and father of the Seiwa Genji's {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|en|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|WD=Q2531241|lt=Minamoto no Mitsunaka}}'s wife. ===Montoku Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Montoku|en|Emperor Montoku|WD=Q357225|lt=Emperor Montoku}}. Among them, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiari|en|Minamoto no Yoshiari|WD=Q11564289|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiari}} was a [[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]], and among his descendants were the [[Sakado clan]] who were [[Hokumen no Bushi]]. ===Seiwa Genji=== {{Main|Seiwa Genji}} These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa}}. The most numerous of them were those descended from {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}}, son of [[Prince Sadazumi]]. {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Hachimantarō Yoshiie}} of the {{ill|Kawachi Genji|en|Kawachi Genji|WD=Q5360652|lt=Kawachi Genji}} was a leader of a ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}''. His descendants set up the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, making his a prestigious pedigree claimed by many ''buke'', particularly for the direct descendants in the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}} (that set up the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}}) and the rival {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta clan}}. Centuries later, {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} would claim descent from the Seiwa Genji by way of the Nitta clan. [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune.jpg|left|thumb|Portrait of [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] (1159–1189)]] ===Yōzei Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Yōzei|en|Emperor Yōzei|WD=Q349280|lt=Emperor Yōzei}}. While {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} is termed the ancestor of the Seiwa Genji, there is evidence (rediscovered in the late 19th century by {{ill|Hoshino Hisashi|en|Hoshino Hisashi|WD=Q724526|lt=Hoshino Hisashi}}) suggesting that he was actually the grandson of Emperor Yōzei rather than of Emperor Seiwa. This theory is not widely accepted as fact, but as Yōzei was deposed for reprehensible behaviour, there would have been a compelling motive to claim descent from more auspicious origins if it were the case. ===Kōkō Genji=== [[File:Minamoto no Tsunemoto.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} (894–961)]] These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Kōkō|en|Emperor Kōkō|WD=Q440518|lt=Emperor Kōkō}}. The great-grandson of his firstborn [[Prince Koretada]], [[Kōshō (sculptor)|Kōshō]], was the ancestor of a line of ''{{ill|Busshi|en|Busshi|WD=Q2928765|lt=Busshi}}'', from which various styles of Buddhist sculpture emerged. Kōshō's grandson [[Kakujo]] established the [[Shichijō Bussho]] workshop. ===Uda Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Uda|en|Emperor Uda|WD=Q349267|lt=Emperor Uda}}. Two sons of [[Prince Atsumi]], {{ill|Minamoto no Masanobu|en|Minamoto no Masanobu|WD=Q3314711|lt=Minamoto no Masanobu}} and [[Minamoto no Shigenobu]] became ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''. Masanobu's children in particular flourished, forming five ''dōjō'' houses as ''[[kuge]]'', and as ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}'' the {{ill|Sasaki clan|en|Sasaki clan|WD=Q1028587|lt=Sasaki clan}} of the [[Ōmi Genji]], and the [[Izumo Genji]]. [[File:Minamoto Yorimitsu.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} (948–1021)]] ===Daigo Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Daigo|en|Emperor Daigo|WD=Q329753|lt=Emperor Daigo}}. His son [[Minamoto no Takaakira]] became a ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]'', but his downfall came during the [[Anna incident]]. Takaakira's descendants include the [[Okamoto clan|Okamoto]] and [[Kawajiri clan|Kawajiri]] clans. Daigo's grandson {{ill|Minamoto no Hiromasa|en|Minamoto no Hiromasa|WD=Q3276201|lt=Minamoto no Hiromasa}} was a reputed musician. ===Murakami Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Murakami|en|Emperor Murakami|WD=Q374015|lt=Emperor Murakami}}. His grandson [[Minamoto no Morofusa|Morofusa]] was an ''[[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]'' and had many descendants, among them several houses of ''dōjō [[kuge]]''. Until the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}} took it during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}, the title of ''[[Genji no Chōja]]'' always fell to one of Morofusa's progeny. [[File:Painting of Minamoto no Sanetomo by Yashima Gakutei, 1825.jpg|thumb|220x220px|Painting of [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]] (1192–1219) – {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura}} {{ill|Minister of the Right|en|Minister of the Right|WD=Q1351174|lt=Udaijin}}]] ===Reizei Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Reizei|en|Emperor Reizei|WD=Q374125|lt=Emperor Reizei}}. Though they are included among the listing of 21 Genji lineages, no concrete record of the names of his descendants made Minamoto is known to survive. ===Kazan Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Kazan}}. They became the ''[[kuge|dōjō]]'' [[Shirakawa family]], which headed the [[Department of Divinities]] for centuries, responsible for the centralised aspects of [[Shinto]]. [[File:Minamoto no Yoshinaka.jpg|left|thumb|A portrait of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|en|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|WD=Q1139202|lt=Minamoto no Yoshinaka}} (1154–1184)]] ===Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Sanjō|en|Emperor Sanjō|WD=Q357231|lt=Emperor Sanjō}}'s son [[Prince Atsuakira]]. Starting with one of them, [[Minamoto no Michisue]], the position of ''Ōkimi-no-kami'' (chief genealogist of the imperial family) in the {{ill|Ministry of the Imperial Household|en|Ministry of the Imperial Household|WD=Q8193428|lt=Ministry of the Imperial Household}} was passed down hereditarily. ===Go-Sanjō Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Go-Sanjō|en|Emperor Go-Sanjō|WD=Q45844|lt=Emperor Go-Sanjō}}'s son [[Prince Sukehito]]. Sukehito's son [[Minamoto no Arihito]] was a ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s vassal [[Tashiro Nobutsuna]], who appears in the ''[[:en:Tale of the Heike|Tale of the Heike]]'', was allegedly Arihito's grandson (according to the ''{{ill|Genpei Jōsuiki|en|Genpei Jōsuiki|WD=Q3020148|lt=Genpei Jōsuiki}}''). [[File:Minamoto no Yoriie (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Minamoto no Yoriie]] (1182–1204)]] ===Go-Shirakawa Genji=== This line consisted solely of {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}} son {{ill|Prince Mochihito|en|Prince Mochihito|WD=Q1941666|lt=Mochihito-ō}} (Takakura-no-Miya). As part of the succession dispute that led to the opening hostilities of the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}}, he was declassed (renamed "[[Minamoto no Mochimitsu]]") and exiled. ===Juntoku Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Juntoku|en|Emperor Juntoku|WD=Q357249|lt=Emperor Juntoku}}'s sons [[Tadanari-ō]] and [[Prince Yoshimune]]. The latter's grandson [[Yotsutsuji Yoshinari|Yoshinari]] rose to ''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]'' with the help of {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|en|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|WD=Q248381|lt=Ashikaga Yoshimitsu}}. [[File:Minamoto Yorinobu.jpg|left|thumb|356x356px|[[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048)]] ===Go-Saga Genji=== This line consisted solely of {{ill|Emperor Go-Saga|en|Emperor Go-Saga|WD=Q349259|lt=Emperor Go-Saga}}'s grandson {{ill|Prince Koreyasu|en|Prince Koreyasu|WD=Q586532|lt=Prince Koreyasu}}. Koreyasu-ō was installed as a puppet ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' (the seventh of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}) at a young age, and was renamed "{{ill|Prince Koreyasu|en|Prince Koreyasu|WD=Q586532|lt=Minamoto no Koreyasu}}" a few years later. After he was deposed, he regained royal status, and became a monk soon after, thereby losing the Minamoto name. [[File:A wooden signboard with a family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) 源氏家紋の丸に笹竜胆付ける木製看板.jpg|thumb|A wooden signboard with a family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) ]] ===Go-Fusakusa Genji=== These were descendants of {{ill|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|en|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|WD=Q349246|lt=Emperor Go-Fukakusa}}'s son {{ill|Prince Hisaaki|en|Prince Hisaaki|WD=Q715826|lt=Prince Hisaaki}} (the eighth ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}). Hisaaki's sons {{ill|Prince Morikuni|en|Prince Morikuni|WD=Q552852|lt=Prince Morikuni}} (the next ''shōgun'') and [[Prince Hisayoshi]] were made Minamoto. Hisayoshi's adopted "nephew" (actually {{ill|Nijō Michihira|en|Nijō Michihira|WD=Q3341478|lt=Nijō Michihira}}'s son) [[Minamoto no Muneaki|Muneaki]] became a ''gon-dainagon'' (acting ''{{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon}}''). ===Ōgimachi Genji=== These were non-royal descendants of {{ill|Emperor Ōgimachi|en|Emperor Ōgimachi|WD=Q334076|lt=Emperor Ōgimachi}}. At first they were ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}'', but they later became ''[[kuge|dōjō-ke]]'', the [[Hirohata family]]. == Legacy == === Historical periods and cities founding === [[File:Kamakura - Grand Bouddha.jpg|thumb|The statue of [[Amitābha|Amida Buddha]] at {{ill|Kōtoku-in|en|Kōtoku-in|WD=Q672056|lt=Kōtoku-in}}, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}]] * {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} and {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura city}}, which were established and founded by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]''—''the first ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' of Japan. * {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} was founded by ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|en|Ashikaga Takauji|WD=Q297107|lt=Ashikaga Takauji}}''—''a direct descendant of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiyasu|en|Minamoto no Yoshiyasu|WD=Q6863161|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiyasu}} (also known as ''Ashikaga Yoshiyasu''). * {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} was founded by ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}''—''who claimed to be a descendant of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshishige|en|Minamoto no Yoshishige|WD=Q732097|lt=Minamoto no Yoshishige}} (also known as ''Nitta Yoshishige''). === Shinto shrines founding === [[File:Rokusonnnou-Jinja shinmon.JPG|thumb|''Shinmon'' of {{ill|Rokusonnō Shrine|en|Rokusonnō Shrine|WD=Q11392320|lt=Rokusonnō Shrine}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}]] * {{Nihongo|{{ill|Three Genji Shrines|en|Three Genji Shrines|WD=Q7797495|lt=Three Genji Shrines}}|源氏三神社|Genji San Jinja}} - A group of Shinto shrines connected closedly with the members of {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} branch of the Minamoto clan. ** {{ill|Rokusonnō Shrine|en|Rokusonnō Shrine|WD=Q11392320|lt=Rokusonnō Shrine}}, {{ill|Minami-ku, Kyoto|en|Minami-ku, Kyoto|WD=Q1154649|lt=Minami-ku}}, Kyoto, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture}} ** [[:en:Tada Jinja|Tada Jinja]], {{ill|Kawanishi, Hyōgo|en|Kawanishi, Hyōgo|WD=Q609350|lt=Kawanishi}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}} ** {{ill|Tsuboi Hachimangū|en|Tsuboi Hachimangū|WD=Q11429677|lt=Tsuboi Hachimangū}}, [[:en:Habikino, Osaka|Habikino]], {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture}} *[[:ja:沙沙貴神社|Sasaki Shrine]] {{Nihongo|2=沙沙貴神社}} - a Shinto shrine connected closely with the members of {{ill|Uda Genji|en|Uda Genji|WD=Q4846201|lt=Uda Genji}} branch of the Minamoto clan. === Literature and arts === [[File:Seated Portrait of Minamoto no Yoritomo (Presumed) 1.jpg|left|thumb|220x220px|Seated Portrait of [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] - {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}} in {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|en|Tokyo National Museum|WD=Q653433|lt=Tokyo National Museum}}]] * {{Nihongo|{{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji}}|源氏物語|Genji monogatari|The Tale of the Minamoto clan}} by {{ill|Murasaki Shikibu|en|Murasaki Shikibu|WD=Q81731|lt=Murasaki Shikibu}}, an important 11th-century classical Japanese novel.[[File:Genji monogatari (ch. 34).jpg|thumb|Genji monogatari]] * {{Nihongo|{{ill|The Tale of the Heike|en|The Tale of the Heike|WD=Q830740|lt=The Tale of the Heike}}|平家物語|Heike Monogatari|The Tale of house of Taira}}'','' a 14th-century {{ill|Epic poetry|en|Epic poetry|WD=Q37484|lt=Epic poetry}} compiled of the struggle between the Minamoto clan and the [[Taira clan]] for control of Japan at the end of the 12th century in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei ''Warrior Rule in Japan'', page 11. Cambridge University Press.{{Cite book |last=井上 |first=辰雄 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_panuAAACAAJ |title=嵯峨天皇と文人官僚 |publisher=塙書房 |year=2011 |isbn=9784827312409 |location=Japan |pages=305–306 |language=ja}} Several noble lines were bestowed the surname, the most notable of which was the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}, whose descendants established the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura}} and {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga}} {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=shogunates}} following the Heian era. The Minamoto was one of the four great [[Japanese clans|clans]] that dominated Japanese politics during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian}} period in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}—the other three were the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]], the [[Taira clan|Taira]], and the {{ill|Tachibana clan (kuge)|en|Tachibana clan (kuge)|WD=Q1500519|lt=Tachibana}}.{{Cite encyclopedia |last=Gibney |first=FRank |year=1984 |title=Shisei: 'Genji' |encyclopedia=Britannica International Encyclopedia |publisher=TBS-Britannica |oclc=47462068}}{{Cite book |last=Frédéric |first=Louis |year=2002 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=9780674017535 |pages=439–452 |language=en}} In the late Heian period, Minamoto rivalry with the Taira culminated in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} (1180–1185 AD). The Minamoto emerged victorious and established Japan's first {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=shogunate}} in {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} under [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], who appointed himself as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' in 1192, ushering in the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} (1192–1333 AD) of Japanese history. The name "Genpei" comes from {{ill|On'yomi|en|On'yomi|WD=Q718498|lt=alternate readings}} of the ''{{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=Kanji}}'' "Minamoto" (源 ''Gen'') and "Taira" (平 ''Hei''). The Kamakura Shogunate was overthrown by {{ill|Emperor Go-Daigo|en|Emperor Go-Daigo|WD=Q313942|lt=Emperor Go-Daigo}} in the [[Kenmu Restoration]] of 1333. Three years later the Kenmu government would then itself be overthrown by the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga clan}}, descendants of the Seiwa Genji who established the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} (1333 to 1573). The Minamoto clan is also called the {{Nihongo|'''Genji'''|源氏|4="Minamoto clan"}}, or less frequently, the {{Nihongo|'''Genke'''|源家|4="House of Minamoto"}}, using the {{ill|On'yomi|en|On'yomi|WD=Q718498|lt=On'yomi}} readings of {{nihongo|''gen''|源}} for "Minamoto", while {{Nihongo|''shi'' or ''ji''|氏}} means "[[Uji (clan)|clan]]", and {{Nihongo|''ke''|家}} is used as a suffix for "{{ill|Extended family|en|Extended family|WD=Q721790|lt=Extended family}}".{{Cite book |last=Lebra |first=Takie Sugiyama |year=1995 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xa0wDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA72 |title=Above the Clouds: Status Culture of the Modern Japanese Nobility |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=9780520076020 |language=en}} == History == The [[:en:Emperors of Japan|Emperors of Japan]] bestowed noble surnames upon members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial family}} who were excluded from the {{ill|List of emperors of Japan|en|List of emperors of Japan|WD=Q188210|lt=line of succession}} and demoted into the Ranks of [[:en:Japanese nobility|the nobility]]. In May 814, the first {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=emperor}} to grant the surname "Minamoto" was {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}, to his seventh son—{{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}}, in [[:en:Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto}}).Frederic, Louis (2002). ''Japan Encyclopedia.'' Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press.{{Cite book |last=倉本 |first=一宏 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3FClzAEACAAJ |title=公家源氏: 王権を支えた名族 |publisher=中央公論新社 |date=2019-12-18 |isbn=9784121025739 |location=Japan |pages=18 |language=ja}}{{rp|18}} The practice was most prevalent during the Heian period (794–1185 AD), although its last occurrence was during the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}. The [[Taira clan|Taira]] were another such offshoot of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=imperial dynasty}}, making both clans distant relatives.{{Cite book |last=Kuehn |first=John T. |title=A military history of Japan: from the age of the Samurai to the 21st century |date=2014 |publisher=Praeger |isbn=978-1-4408-0394-9 |location=Santa Barbara, Calif. |pages=36}} [[File:Seiryoji0332.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Seiryō-ji|en|Seiryō-ji|WD=Q534101|lt=Seiryō-ji}}, a temple in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, was once a villa of {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Minamoto no Tōru}} (d. 895), a prominent member of the Saga Genji|left]]The most prominent of the several Minamoto families, the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}, descended from {{ill|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|en|Minamoto no Tsunemoto|WD=Q3099236|lt=Minamoto no Tsunemoto}} (897–961), a grandson of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa}}. Tsunemoto went to the provinces and became the founder of a major warrior dynasty. {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|en|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|WD=Q2531241|lt=Minamoto no Mitsunaka}} (912–997) formed an alliance with the Fujiwara. Thereafter the Fujiwara frequently called upon the Minamoto to restore order in the capital, [[:en:Heian-Kyo|Heian-Kyō]] (modern {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyōto}}).{{rp|240–241}}Mitsunaka's eldest son, {{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} (948–1021), became the protégé of {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}; another son, [[Minamoto no Yorinobu]] (968–1048) suppressed the rebellion of {{ill|Taira no Tadatsune|en|Taira no Tadatsune|WD=Q1105844|lt=Taira no Tadatsune}} in 1032. Yorinobu's son, [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988–1075), and grandson, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1039–1106), pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0804705232 |pages=241–242, 247–252}} [[File:Emperor Saga.jpg|left|thumb|399x399px|{{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}} (786 – 842)]] The Seiwa Genji's fortunes declined in the [[:en:Hōgen Rebellion|Hōgen Rebellion]] (1156), when the Taira executed most of the line, including {{ill|Minamoto no Tameyoshi|en|Minamoto no Tameyoshi|WD=Q1381638|lt=Minamoto no Tameyoshi}}. During the [[:en:Heiji Disturbance|Heiji Disturbance]] (1160), the head of the Seiwa Genji, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}}, died in battle.{{rp|256–258}} [[Taira no Kiyomori]] seized power in Kyoto by forging an alliance with the retired emperors {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Go-Shirakawa}} and {{ill|Emperor Toba|en|Emperor Toba|WD=Q349284|lt=Toba}} and infiltrating the ''[[kuge]]''. He sent [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (1147–1199), the third son of Minamoto no Yoshimoto of the Seiwa Genji, into exile. In 1180, during the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}}, Yoritomo mounted a full-scale rebellion against the Taira rule, culminating in the destruction of the Taira and the subjugation of eastern Japan within five years. In 1192, he received the title ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' and set up the first ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' in the history of Japan at {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}—{{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}.{{rp|275,259–260, 289–305,331}} [[File:Minamoto no Makoto.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Minamoto no Makoto}} (810 – 868)]] The later {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga}} (founders of the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} of {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}), [[:en:Nitta family|Nitta]], [[:en:Takeda family|Takeda]], and [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]] (founders of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] of {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}) clans claim descents from the during the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} ]] The {{ill|protagonist|en|protagonist|WD=Q215972|lt=protagonist}} of the classical Japanese novel ''{{ill|The Tale of Genji|en|The Tale of Genji|WD=Q8269|lt=The Tale of Genji}} (The Tale of Minamoto clan)—''{{ill|Hikaru Genji|en|Hikaru Genji|WD=Q997646|lt=Hikaru Genji}}, was bestowed the name Minamoto for political reasons by his father the emperor and was delegated to civilian life and a career as an imperial officer. The {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War}} is also the subject of the early Japanese epic ''{{ill|The Tale of the Heike|en|The Tale of the Heike|WD=Q830740|lt=The Tale of the Heike}}'' (''Heike Monogatari'').{{Cite book|last1=Watson|first1=Burton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF4aAwAAQBAJ|title=The Tales of the Heike|last2=Shirane|first2=Haruo|date=2006-06-27|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-51083-7|pages=4|language=en}} == Members of the Minamoto clan (Genji clan) == Even within {{ill|Royal family|en|Royal family|WD=Q2006518|lt=royalty}} there was a distinction between princes with the title {{nihongo3||親王|shinnō}}, who could ascend to the throne, and princes with the title {{nihongo3||王|ō}}, who were not members of the line of imperial succession but nevertheless remained members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=royal class}} (and therefore outRanked members of Minamoto clans). The bestowing of the Minamoto name on a (theretofore-)prince or his descendants excluded them from the royal class altogether, thereby operating as a reduction in legal and social Rank even for ''ō''-princes not previously in the line of succession. [[File:Old silver coin with family crest of Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji), Edo period.png|left|thumb|291x291px|{{ill|Silver coin|en|Silver coin|WD=Q610038|lt=Old silver coin}} with [[Mon (emblem)|mon]](emblem) of the Minamoto clan (Seiwa Genji), found in {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}]] Many later clans were formed by members of the Minamoto clan, and in many early cases, progenitors of these clans are known by either family name. There are also known {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=monks}} of Minamoto descent; these are often noted in genealogies but did not carry the clan name (in favour of a {{ill|Dharma name|en|Dharma name|WD=Q1543672|lt=Dharma name}}). [[File:Kabuto attached with family crest of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou) 源氏家紋の笹竜胆付ける兜.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kabuto|en|Kabuto|WD=Q1720878|lt=Kabuto}} attached with [[Mon (emblem)|Mon]] (emblem) of Minamoto clan (sasa-rindou)]] The Minamoto is the ancestor and parent clan of many notable descendant clans, some of which are {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga}}, [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]], {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira}}, {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta}}, [[Takeda clan|Takeda]], {{ill|Shimazu clan|en|Shimazu clan|WD=Q1061406|lt=Shimazu}}, {{ill|Sasaki clan|en|Sasaki clan|WD=Q1028587|lt=Sasaki}}, {{ill|Akamatsu clan|en|Akamatsu clan|WD=Q2659667|lt=Akamatsu}}, [[Kitabatake clan|Kitabatake]], Tada, {{ill|Ōta clan|en|Ōta clan|WD=Q1391922|lt=Ota}}, [[Toki clan|Toki]], {{ill|Yamana clan|en|Yamana clan|WD=Q2975406|lt=Yamana}}, {{ill|Satomi clan|en|Satomi clan|WD=Q2975367|lt=Satomi}}, {{ill|Hosokawa clan|en|Hosokawa clan|WD=Q2736120|lt=Hosokawa}}, {{ill|Satake clan|en|Satake clan|WD=Q2975363|lt=Satake}}, Yamamoto, Hemi, {{ill|Ogasawara clan|en|Ogasawara clan|WD=Q2975340|lt=Ogasawara}}, {{ill|Yasuda clan|en|Yasuda clan|WD=Q8049951|lt=Yasuda}}, Takenouchi, Hiraga, [[Imagawa clan|Imagawa]], {{ill|Miyake clan|en|Miyake clan|WD=Q2975320|lt=Miyake}}, etc.{{Cite book |last=Papinot |first=Jacques Edmond Joseph |url=http://www.unterstein.net/Toyoashihara-no-Chiaki-Nagaioaki-no-Mitsuho-no-Kuni/NobiliaireJapon.pdf |title=Nobiliaire du Japon |publisher=Oliver Rost; Stefan Unterstein |year=1906 |location=Dortmund; München |pages=3–73 |language=fr}} There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=the emperor}} from whom it descended. Some of these lineages were populous, but a few did not produce descendants. ===Saga Genji=== The Saga Genji are descendants of {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}}. As Saga had many children, many were bestowed the ''{{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=uji}}'' Minamoto, declassing them from imperial succession. Among his sons, {{ill|Minamoto no Makoto|en|Minamoto no Makoto|WD=Q6863142|lt=Makoto}}, [[Minamoto no Tokiwa|Tokiwa]], and {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|en|Minamoto no Tōru|WD=Q1284268|lt=Tōru}} took the position of Minister of the Left (''[[:en:Sadaijin|Sadaijin]]''); they were among the most powerful in the Imperial Court in the early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}. Some of Tōru's descendants in particular settled the provinces and formed ''{{ill|Buke (Japan)|en|Buke (Japan)|WD=Q2927809|lt=buke}}''. Clans such as the {{ill|Watanabe|en|Watanabe|WD=Q10983405|lt=Watanabe}}, [[Matsuura clan|Matsuura]], and [[Kamachi clan|Kamachi]] descend from the Saga Genji.{{Cite book |url=http://www.daiichi-g.co.jp/kokugo/textbook/data/KA_316/KA_316_hs.pdf |title=高等学校 改訂版 古典Ａ 大鏡 源氏物語 諸家の文章 |publisher=株式会社第一学習社 |year=2018 |isbn=978-4-8040-1075-5 |edition=4th |pages=43–56
